name: Quechua Ancash-Huailas: Callejón de Huailas variety
confidence_why: Parker 1976 and the independently written Levengood & Larsen 1982 both describe Callejón de Huaylas Quechua stress as weight-conditioned with an initial default (heavy syllable attracts stress, otherwise the first syllable), whereas Julca-Guerrero 2010 asserts fixed penultimate stress but lists as 'exceptions' exactly the light-penult words (wáraka, kályana, číkuti, túnquri) that the other two descriptions predict to be initially stressed.

new_statements.quote: 2.4. La Acentuación. Las palabras pronunciadas aisladamente son en general acentuadas de acuerdo a las siguientes pautas: palabras mono y bisílabas, y palabras trisílabas con una penúltima sílaba abierta, tienen una acentuación primaria inicial. Palabras trisílabas con una penúltima sílaba cerrada y todas las palabras cuatrisílabas tienen acentuación secundaria sobre la sílaba inicial y acentuación primaria sobre la penúltima. Ejemplos: ['kan] 'hay', ['kani] 'muerdéle!', ['imataq] 'qué?' [ˌwa'ra:nin] 'al dia siguiente' [ˌnoqa'no:mi] 'él es como yo'. Las pautas de acentuación en palabras de más de cuatro sílabas no han sido definidas todavía.
new_statements.translation: 2.4. Stress. Words pronounced in isolation are in general stressed according to the following patterns: mono- and disyllabic words, and trisyllabic words with an open penultimate syllable, have primary stress on the initial syllable. Trisyllabic words with a closed penultimate syllable and all four-syllable words have secondary stress on the initial syllable and primary stress on the penult. Examples: ['kan] 'there is', ['kani] 'bite him!', ['imataq] 'what?', [ˌwa'ra:nin] 'the next day', [ˌnoqa'no:mi] 'he is like me'. The stress patterns of words of more than four syllables have not yet been determined.

Reading: weight-sensitive is right — initial primary stress in 1-3 syllable words unless a trisyllable's penult is heavy, then penult primary + initial se…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-hedged Parker 1976 reading (heavy syllable attracts stress, otherwise initial stress in isolated/clause-final words) and independent of it (written 1972, before Parker 1976). It adds what the catalog lacks: explicit initial secondary stress, and an explicit statement that light-penult trisyllables are initially stressed (['imataq]). It diverges from Parker in one detail: it says ALL four-syllable words take penult primary stress regardless of weight (Parker would predict initial stress in a four-syllable word with no non-final heavy syllable), and it looks only at the penult's weight, not at any non-final heavy syllable. It contradicts the fixed: penulti…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For words in isolation: primary stress is initial in one-, two- and three-syllable words unless the penult of a trisyllable is heavy (closed, or long-vowelled as in wa'ra:nin), in which case the penult takes primary stress; all four-syllable words have penult primary stress; longer words undescribed. Penult weight decides between initial and penultimate stress in trisyllables. §2.5 adds a phrase-level fact: the penultimate syllable of a declarative sentence carries the sentence's highest pitch, and the final syllable a fall.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the initial syllable whenever primary stress is on the penult (trisyllables with a heavy penult and all four-syllable words), e.g. [ˌwa'ra:nin], [ˌnoqa'no:mi].
new_statements.exceptions: Words of more than four syllables: patterns 'not yet defined'. The description is limited to words pronounced in isolation; no lexical exceptions are given. The sketch was written in 1972 for Les Langues du Monde (prologue, p. iii), with principal informants from Atipayán (Huaraz province) and Shumay near Marcará (Carhuaz); it notes that dialect differences north of Marcará and south of Huaraz were not described (§1.1.1, p. 1).
new_statements.identity_note: Levengood & Larsen 1982 describes 'quechua de Huaylas' as spoken west of the Cordillera Blanca (provinces of Huaylas, Yungay, Carhuaz, Huaraz, Aija, Recuay and NE Bolognesi), citing Parker p. 27; principal informants from Atipayán (Huaraz) and Shumay near Marcará (Carhuaz), i.e. the Callejón de Huaylas lect of the catalog record. Hammer et al. 1992 is explicitly 'Quechua del Callejón de Huaylas'. The additionally saved 2000 guide (Easthouse et al.) is the South Conchucos Quechua adaptation and is not about this language.

readall_conflicts: Levengood & Larsen 1982 (written 1972) and the catalog's Parker 1976 agree that stress in Huaylas Quechua is weight-conditioned with an initial default: a light-penult trisyllable is initially stressed (['imataq]) and a heavy penult draws primary stress ([ˌwa'ra:nin]). They differ on four-syllable words: Levengood & Larsen give penult primary plus initial secondary for all of them, while Parker's rule (first non-final heavy syllable, else initial) would put the stress initially in an all-light four-syllable word; Levengood & Larsen also do not mention Parker's clause-internal versus clause-final distinction. Both disagree with Julca-Guerrero 2010 (fixed penult, already listed as 'contra' in our check), which predicts i'mataq. Hammer et al. 1992 is silent.

tone.quote: Accentual phenomena in Huaylas are more complex than in most forms of Quechua, and are not thoroughly understood at present. The basic rule for accent placement is that higher pitch and greater length accompany the first syllable of each word, except that in the last, i.e. nuclear, word of the sentence or non-embedded clause this accent falls on the last non-final long syllable (viz. one that ends in a consonant or long vowel). Intonational phenomena are obviously involved here, and there is the added complication that pitch and length are dissociated in sequences of three or more short ((C)V) syllables; for further details and examples see Parker 1967a.
tone.locator: sec. 2 'The Systematic Phonemes of Huaylas Quechua', typescript p. 5 = p. 147
tone.summary: No lexical tone: pitch is named only as a correlate (with length) of a positional word accent - word-initial by default, last non-final heavy syllable in the clause-final word - with pitch/length dissociation in light-syllable runs attributed to intonation.
